extracted.intended_audience: readers of satirical fiction / literary scholars
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from Samuel Butler's satirical novel Erewhon (Victorian-era prose) describing the fictional country's social, legal, and moral conventions — useful as source material for satire/humor analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valorisation of fair hair
rubrics_metrics.description: Having fair (light) hair is reckoned a very great merit, greatly admired and envied; light hair and complexion may influence how authorities treat a stranger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The narrator’s light hair and complexion were repeatedly noticed and helped to mollify officials; having 'such a good character (they meant physique), and such beautiful light hair' contributed to leniency and even to receiving a pension. Implication: physical traits operate as social credentials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession of foreign machinery (watch) treated as contraband
rubrics_metrics.description: Possession of certain mechanical devices (e.g., a watch) is regarded with suspicion; such items may be confiscated and can trigger official action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Narrator’s watch was seized; magistrate considered it damaging. Confiscated machines may be welcomed by the metropolitan museum of old machines. Possession can result in detention while the government is consulted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illness criminalized for people under seventy
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person falls into ill health or 'fails bodily' before age seventy, they are tried before a jury and, if convicted, held up to public scorn and sentenced (severity varies with the illness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details: Subdivisions of illnesses exist into 'crimes' and 'misdemeanours' analogous to legal offences; serious illness incurs heavy punishment, lesser physical failures in older people may lead only to fines or light penalties. Example: two men had been imprisoned with hard labour for being 'in ill health.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral crimes medicalized and treated sympathetically
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts considered criminal in the narrator’s home country (forgery, arson, robbery) are treated as medical/moral disorders in Erewhon and often result in care rather than punishment; wealthy offenders may publicly declare their 'immorality' to receive sympathy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: A forger or robber might be taken to a hospital and carefully tended at public expense; a rich man announces he is 'suffering from a severe fit of immorality' to elicit visitors and sympathy. The society tends to ascribe moral defects to misfortune or mischance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical appearance influences legal and social outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical attributes (hair colour, eye colour, fresh complexion, general physique) significantly affect legal fate, mercy, and public reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Queen petitioned the King to pardon the narrator and assign a pension 'in consideration of your meritorious complexion.' Good looks also draw crowds, hospitality, and invitations. Appearance functions as a de facto merit metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition and strict prohibition of machinery and invention
rubrics_metrics.description: After acceptance of an influential book that machines would supplant humans, the country destroyed/discarded machines not used for more than two hundred and seventy-one years and forbade further improvements and inventions under severe legal fiction (equating invention with disease).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details: Legally, making new machines or improvements is condemned, and transgression is equated with having 'typhus fever' — one of the worst crimes. The old machines are preserved in a museum and ticketed, but active mechanical innovation is outlawed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflation of mental and physical disease as legal fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The society formally conflates mental and physical diseases for legal and social purposes, using such fictions to justify laws (e.g., equating inventiveness with typhus fever).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The text explicitly notes that equating inventions with typhus fever is an avowed legal fiction. This conflation underpins criminalization/medicalization practices and justifies state interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'straighteners' as professional moral/medical authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist specialized practitioners ('straighteners') whose role is to treat or 'straighten' moral/mental deviations; their authority can induce strong emotional/physical responses and social treatments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: A family straightener attends Mr. Nosnibor and prescribes treatment resulting in weeping and wailing; straighteners are found among the graduates of the Colleges of Unreason and occupy social positions (managers, priests, etc.). They mediate what counts as illness or moral failing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of persons by wealth as 'horse-power'
rubrics_metrics.description: People are classed and spoken of by the number of foot-pounds or 'horse-power' they can raise (a local metric of wealth/power).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mr. Nosnibor is described as 'a man of at least 500,000 horse-power' and that metric is used to indicate social standing and influence, e.g., who 'keeps a capital table' and 'stands higher' in society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different institutional responses based on status and circumstance
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses to illness or wrongdoing vary by social status and other conditions: the rich may receive care/sympathy, older people minor penalties, while others face imprisonment with hard labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Serious illness in a younger person may result in public scorn and prison; wealthy wrongdoers are publicly tended and may advertise their immorality to gain sympathy; the narrator’s possible punishment was mitigated by his appearance and stranger status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public spectacle economy around prisoners/curiosities
rubrics_metrics.description: Prisoners and curiosities attract visitors who pay fees; the populace is eager to see unusual persons, and hosts may profit by permitting viewings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: People from the town pester the jailor to see the narrator and are admitted upon payment of handsome fees; the narrator is treated as an object of interest and given receptions during travel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social intolerance for 'ill-luck' as offensive
rubrics_metrics.description: Ill luck, misfortune, or ill-treatment that would merit sympathy elsewhere is considered offensive and is regarded as an 'offence against society' because it makes people uncomfortable to hear of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The society will not accept pleas based on misfortune; they ascribe moral defects to misfortune when convenient, yet reject pleas of bad luck that would elsewhere elicit sympathy. This shapes social judgment and legal outcomes.
